clue.text: Paris producer welcoming youngster into part of theatre

indicators.note: welcoming means one piece takes the other in, like a host letting a guest inside
part of says only a run of letters from inside the word theatre is wanted

parts.note: a cub is a young animal, and by extension a youngster

explanation.surface: A theatrical producer called Paris lets a young newcomer into a corner of the playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paris producer' reads as a theatre impresario named Paris, but it means the person who gave birth to Paris of Troy: his mother, queen of Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Hecuba, queen of Troy, was the mother of Paris, so she literally produced him.

clue.text: Unsophisticated Foreign Secretary's play on words on words

parts.note: Sir Alec Douglas-Home was British Foreign Secretary; Home's gives HOMES
a pun is a play on words

explanation.surface: A simple joke by a senior government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas-Home is pronounced 'Hume' but spelt HOME; the possessive gives the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Homespun means simple and plain, without refinement, so unsophisticated.

clue.text: Responsible person's occupation out East

indicators.note: out means the letter goes out of the word

parts.note: a career is an occupation

explanation.surface: A responsible job, but with the eastern part gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A carer looks after someone sick or elderly, a person responsible for them.

clue.text: Stole last of meat from galley, perhaps

indicators.note: from here means taken away from, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a galley is one kind of boat

indicators.note: last of means the final letter of the word meat

explanation.surface: Someone pinched the remaining meat from the ship's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stole' looks like a verb but is the wrap; 'galley' looks like the kitchen but is the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A boa is a long fluffy scarf worn round the neck, a type of stole.

clue.text: Festival swineherd always observed

parts.note: a swineherd is a man who looks after hogs: a hog man
ay (aye) is an old poetic word for always

explanation.surface: A pig keeper never misses the annual celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: HOGMANAY is the Scottish New Year's Eve celebration. 'observed' is a link word, nodding at a festival being kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogmanay is the Scottish name for the New Year's Eve festivities, a festival in its own right.

clue.text: Supervise deliveries, taking escort

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries
to see someone home is to escort them

explanation.surface: Overseeing deliveries while accompanying someone.
explanation.walkthrough: An over in cricket is six balls bowled, the deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee is to watch over and direct work, which is to supervise it.

clue.text: Behave ostentatiously, having just left the board?

definitions.meaning: to draw attention to oneself showily
a diver who has just left the diving board is about to hit the water

explanation.surface: Showing off as one leaves a committee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the board' suggests a company board, but it is a diving board.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a splash is an idiom for attracting attention flamboyantly, or literally hitting water.

clue.text: Coinage in Limoges — and no mistake

indicators.note: mistake as an imperative means get these letters wrong, rearranging them

explanation.surface: An error in the French porcelain town, clearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and no mistake' reads as an emphatic phrase but signals rearranging LIMOGES plus NO.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly coined word, so a coinage in the linguistic sense.

clue.text: Rabbit on part of ferry at terminal

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A creature hops aboard a boat at the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is British slang for chatter, as in rabbit on.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabbit and yatter are both informal words for chattering on at length.

clue.text: Not solidly grounded, a month before retiring

parts.note: Mar is the abbreviation for March
retiring means shy or reserved

explanation.surface: Unsteady for a month before withdrawing.
explanation.definitionFit: Marshy ground is soft and boggy, literally not solid underfoot.

clue.text: Preserve and equip a youth feeding a setter

indicators.note: feeding means the following pieces go into the mouth of the other piece

parts.note: a crossword setter refers to themself as me
to arm is to equip with weapons
a lad is a youth

explanation.surface: Someone is told to keep things, arm a young man, and give a gun dog its dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like the gun dog, but in crosswords the setter is the compiler, who speaks of themself in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmalade is a citrus preserve, the jam-like spread eaten on toast.

clue.text: Whip early king used to restrain love

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: Knut (Canute) was an early king of England in the eleventh century
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch used a lash to keep romance in check.
explanation.definitionFit: A knout is a Russian scourge or lash, a type of whip used for flogging.

clue.text: Broadly, Jean Rhys's source of floating algae?

definitions.text: Broadly, Jean Rhys's source of floating algae?

parts.words: Broadly, Jean Rhys's source of floating algae?
parts.note: Broadly hints at wide, and the remainder describes an Atlantic region thick with floating seaweed

explanation.surface: A loose description of where the novelist found her seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip WIDE (from 'Broadly') off the title of Jean Rhys's novel Wide Sargasso Sea and you have the area of the Atlantic known for floating sargassum weed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic famous for mats of floating sargassum seaweed.

clue.text: Very cheap aid organised by fellows snatching a nap

indicators.note: organised means the letters of aid are put in a new order
snatching means grabbing something and holding it inside

parts.note: men are fellows
a doze is a short sleep, a nap

explanation.surface: Charity arranged by men who sneak a quick sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' rearranges AID into ADI.
explanation.definitionFit: A dime a dozen is an idiom for something so plentiful it is very cheap.

clue.text: Leading cardinal was most successful in speech

indicators.note: in speech says the word is heard spoken, not seen written

parts.note: to have won is to have been most successful in a contest

explanation.surface: A senior churchman who came top in a debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cardinal' suggests a churchman but means a cardinal number; the first of them leads.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardinal numbers count one, two, three; the first or leading one is one.

clue.text: Lack of purpose, cutting off head's gas, for example

indicators.note: cutting off the head means removing the first letter of the word

parts.note: futility is pointlessness, a lack of purpose

explanation.surface: Something pointless lops off the top of a gas supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas is an example of a utility, a public service such as water, electricity or gas.

clue.text: Accommodating type shot outside tower

indicators.note: outside means the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: an inner is a shot hitting the ring next to the bull on a target
a keep is the main tower of a castle

explanation.surface: A helpful person fires at a castle tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accommodating' looks like 'obliging' but means providing rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: An innkeeper runs an inn, a type of person who provides accommodation.

clue.text: Lively wit runs into European bank

indicators.note: into means one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: a spit is a narrow bank of sand jutting into the sea
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A sparkling humorist dashes into a bank on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Esprit, borrowed from French, means liveliness of mind and sparkling wit.

clue.text: Possible customer's outlook

definitions.meaning: the view or what lies ahead

explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is both a likely client and a view or expectation of the future.

clue.text: Fanciful as a French coin once used in Spain

parts.note: un is the French for a
the real was a former Spanish silver coin

explanation.surface: An imaginary story about a French coin that once circulated in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unreal is imaginary or not genuine, much as a fanciful notion is.

clue.text: Row over unacceptable rugby formation

parts.note: a row is a line
out means not acceptable, as in that idea is out

explanation.surface: An argument over a disallowed move in a rugby game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like an argument but is a line. A lineout is the rugby set piece where forwards line up for a throw-in.
explanation.definitionFit: A lineout restarts play in rugby union with two lines of forwards, a rugby formation.

clue.text: To merely exist, some feel, breaks one of its rules!

definitions.text: To merely exist, some feel, breaks one of its rules!

parts.words: To merely exist, some feel, breaks one of its rules!
parts.note: the phrase to merely exist splits an infinitive, which purists feel breaks a rule of correct language usage

explanation.surface: A complaint that simply existing breaks the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue demonstrates its own point: 'To merely exist' puts 'merely' between 'to' and 'exist', a split infinitive.
explanation.definitionFit: The ban on splitting infinitives is a traditional rule of English grammar, though many dispute it.

clue.text: One of a thousand in the fillies' race?

definitions.text: One of a thousand in the fillies' race?

parts.words: One of a thousand in the fillies' race?
parts.note: the 1000 ... is a classic English horse race for fillies, so one of the thousand is a single coin of that name

explanation.surface: A single runner in a big race for young female horses.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1000 Guineas is a Newmarket classic for fillies; the old guinea was a British gold coin worth 21 shillings.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1000 Guineas race is named for guineas, so one of the thousand is a single old gold coin.

clue.text: Free deserter arrested by private soldiers

indicators.note: arrested by means held inside the next piece

parts.note: GIs are American private soldiers
a rat is one who deserts, as rats leave a sinking ship

explanation.surface: Ordinary troops detain a runaway at no charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratis means without charge, that is free of cost.

clue.text: Act like one of eight, say, seeing deer

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken aloud and sounds like another

parts.note: one of a rowing eight must row

explanation.surface: Someone imitating a member of a crew spots a deer.
explanation.walkthrough: An eight is a racing boat with eight oarsmen; to act like one is to ROW.
explanation.definitionFit: The roe is a small Eurasian species of deer.

clue.text: Pedantry of Chesterton's remote and ineffectual attacker?

definitions.text: Pedantry of Chesterton's remote and ineffectual attacker?

parts.words: Pedantry of Chesterton's remote and ineffectual attacker?
parts.note: Hilaire Belloc's Lines to a Don addressed a remote and ineffectual Don who dared attack his friend Chesterton; the quality of such an academic is pedantry

explanation.surface: The fussiness of a critic who went after G. K. Chesterton.
explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's poem opens 'Remote and ineffectual Don / That dared attack my Chesterton'; the answer is the quality of being like a don.
explanation.definitionFit: Donnishness is the pedantic, bookish manner of a university don, hence pedantry.

clue.text: Bondsman ultimately slain in overthrow of republic

indicators.note: in means the last letter sits inside the turned word
overthrow of means turning the word upside down, read upwards in a down clue

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for the Republic of Ireland

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of slain

explanation.surface: A bound servant finally killed in a revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overthrow of' turns EIRE into ERIE; N, the end of 'slain', goes in. ERNIE is the machine picking Premium Bond winners in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: ERNIE is the random number machine that draws Premium Bond prizes, so a Bondsman in a playful sense.

clue.text: Precious stone presented to Mexican poet

parts.note: Octavio Paz was a Mexican poet and Nobel laureate

explanation.surface: A jewel given as a gift to a Latin American writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Topaz is a gemstone, often yellow, prized as a precious stone in jewellery.

clue.text: Honour a new church, holding one's act of homage

indicators.note: holding means the first group of pieces keeps the other piece inside it

parts.note: the OBE (Order of the British Empire) is a British honour
CE is the Church of England
one is I, and 's stands for is, giving I then S

explanation.surface: A newly decorated person pays respect at a new church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's' is read as 'one is': I + S, the abbreviated 's spelling IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeisance is a gesture of deference such as a bow, an act of homage.

clue.text: Old man associated with southern resort

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: A father heading off to a holiday town in the south.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa is a resort town with mineral springs.

clue.text: Right woman in group to introduce a piece of music

indicators.note: in means the right and woman pieces sit inside the group

parts.note: a set is a group
Ena is a woman's name

explanation.surface: The proper lady in a gathering is about to present an item of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A serenata is an eighteenth-century cantata or instrumental suite, a piece of music like a serenade.

clue.text: Transparent case leader of investigation dropped

indicators.note: dropped means that letter is removed from the word

parts.note: a patient is a case to a doctor

indicators.note: leader of means the first letter of the word investigation

explanation.surface: An open-and-shut case after the chief investigator was taken off it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks legal but is medical: a doctor's case is a PATIENT, from which the I goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent means plain or obvious, as in a patent lie, so it is transparent.
